records.title: A child mill worker's two-mile walk in the dark
records.occupation: Doffer in a flax mill, from the age of six
records.dateLabel: Described in evidence given in 1832 (about earlier years; the exact years are not given in this transcript)

origin.place: Home, about two miles from the mill
origin.note: The testimony gives a distance, not an address.

destination.note: Hunslet is named in the testimony; the mill's site isn't given in this transcript. Marker at Leeds' representative point.

records.account: Giving evidence in 1832, Bentley said she started work as a little doffer at six, lived two miles from the mill and her family had no clock. Her mother got up around 4 a.m. to make sure she was on time. She described waiting at Hunslet Car at 2 a.m. in the rain until the mill opened, and said that a quarter of an hour's lateness cost half an hour's pay.
records.quote: Did you live far from the mill? — Yes, two miles.

sources.title: Testimony before the Sadler Committee, 1832 (transcribed extract)
sources.institution: Select Committee on the Factories Bill (Sadler Committee), British Parliamentary Papers 1831–32; extract published by Macmillan Learning

records.caveats: Evidence collected by a committee campaigning to limit children's hours. It describes one witness's experience, not a measured commute.

records.title: The City of London: 13,709 by night, 436,721 by day
records.person: People enumerated in, or working in, the City of London

origin.note: Marker placed in the City; the figures cover the whole City.

records.account: The 1921 Census was the first in England and Wales to ask for each worker's place of work. The General Report describes the City of London as almost completely non-residential: a night (enumerated) population of 13,709 and a day population of 436,721, more than thirty times as large. It estimates that central London gained rather more than 800,000 people during the day, about half of them going to the City.
records.quote: more than thirty times as large day population of 436,721

sources.title: 1921 Census of England and Wales, General Report with Appendices, Part XI: Workplaces
sources.institution: General Register Office (HMSO); transcription by A Vision of Britain through Time, University of Portsmouth

records.caveats: Day population counts people with 'no fixed workplace' or no stated workplace as working where they were enumerated, and excludes shoppers and visitors. The census was postponed to 19 June 1921, when some people were away on holiday, and unemployed people were asked for their last workplace.

records.title: Early workmen's fares and an hour's wait before work
records.person: Workers using workmen's trams and trains into central London (a group)

origin.note: The question doesn't name where the workers came from.

destination.note: Area marker only; no specific workplace is named.

records.account: Major Salmon MP said many workers who, for economic reasons, used cheap workmen's trams and trains to reach central London arrived early and often waited idle, sometimes in bad weather, for up to an hour before starting work, because workmen's tickets were only issued until about 7.30 a.m. He asked for this to be extended to 8 a.m. The Minister of Transport, Colonel Ashley, declined, citing the risk of congestion between 8 and 9 a.m.
records.quote: as much as an hour before commencing work

sources.title: House of Commons: Railways and Tramways (Workmen's Tickets)
sources.institution: UK Parliament, Hansard

records.caveats: A question in Parliament describing a general situation. It gives no counts.

records.title: 'Travelling' underground: the unpaid walk to the coal face
records.person: Coal miners, as observed by George Orwell
records.mode: On foot underground, stooping, after the cage ride down the shaft
records.frequency: Every shift, as Orwell describes it
records.duration: About 20 minutes a mile for an experienced miner; at least an hour a day in total, often two or three

origin.note: Orwell based his mining research around Wigan. The chapter doesn't name the pits, so this is an area marker.

records.account: Orwell describes the journey from the bottom of the shaft to the coal face. He says it was often a mile, three miles was fairly normal and in a few mines it was up to five, walked bent double. Miners weren't paid for this 'travelling', which added at least an hour to the working day. This is travel inside the workplace rather than a commute from home, but it shaped the length of a miner's working day.
records.quote: three miles is a fairly normal one

sources.title: The Road to Wigan Pier, chapter 2 ('Down the Mine')
sources.author: George Orwell
sources.institution: Victor Gollancz (Left Book Club); online text copy

records.caveats: A writer's description of mines he visited, not a survey.

origin.note: Place names are anonymised in the published research, so this record isn't placed on the map.

records.account: In 1954 B's diary records catching the 7.45 bus to work, and walking to a bus stop for another bus. From about 1958 she mostly cycled. From 1964 she drove the roughly 3 km to work. On 18 March 1968 she had to cycle because the car had a flat tyre.
records.quote: I walked to NH for 5 to 10 bus
